claim: Replicative helicases in all cell types are hexameric rings that unwind DNA by steric exclusion.
source: Replicative helicases in all cell types are hexameric rings that unwind DNA by steric exclusion in which the helicase encircles the tracking strand only and excludes the other strand from the ring.
evidence: This is a general statement about helicase structure and mechanism that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Steric exclusion mode of helicases involves encircling the tracking strand only and excluding the other strand from the ring.
source: Replicative helicases in all cell types are hexameric rings that unwind DNA by steric exclusion in which the helicase encircles the tracking strand only and excludes the other strand from the ring.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of steric exclusion based on established knowledge of helicase function.

claim: Steric exclusion mode allows helicases to bypass blocks on the strand that is excluded from the central channel.
source: This mode of translocation allows helicases to bypass blocks on the strand that is excluded from the central channel.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the steric exclusion mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: Eukaryotic CMG helicase partially encircles duplex DNA at a forked junction.
source: Unlike other replicative helicases, eukaryotic CMG helicase partially encircles duplex DNA at a forked junction and is stopped by a block on the non-tracking (lagging) strand.
evidence: This is supported by structural data referenced in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CMG helicase is stopped by a block on the non-tracking (lagging) strand.
source: Unlike other replicative helicases, eukaryotic CMG helicase partially encircles duplex DNA at a forked junction and is stopped by a block on the non-tracking (lagging) strand.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript and references to prior work.

claim: Mcm10 is an essential replication protein unique to eukaryotes.
source: This report demonstrates that Mcm10, an essential replication protein unique to eukaryotes, binds CMG and greatly stimulates its helicase activity in vitro.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mcm10 supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Mcm10 binds CMG and greatly stimulates its helicase activity in vitro.
source: This report demonstrates that Mcm10, an essential replication protein unique to eukaryotes, binds CMG and greatly stimulates its helicase activity in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mcm10 enables CMG and the replisome to bypass blocks on the non-tracking DNA strand.
source: Most significantly, Mcm10 enables CMG and the replisome to bypass blocks on the non-tracking DNA strand.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Bypass of lagging strand blocks by CMG-Mcm10 occurs without displacement of the blocks.
source: We demonstrate that bypass occurs without displacement of the blocks and therefore Mcm10 must isomerize the CMG-DNA complex to achieve the bypass function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6 showing streptavidin remains bound to DNA after bypass.

claim: Mcm10 must isomerize the CMG-DNA complex to achieve the bypass function.
source: We demonstrate that bypass occurs without displacement of the blocks and therefore Mcm10 must isomerize the CMG-DNA complex to achieve the bypass function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocks are bypassed without displacement.

claim: There are four superfamilies of hexameric helicases, SF3-6.
source: There are four superfamilies of hexameric helicases, SF3-6, that assort into two main groups, the bacterial helicases (SF4,5) that have ATP sites derived from the RecA fold and the eukaryotic/archaeal helicases (SF3,6) that have ATP sites derived from the AAA+ fold (Singleton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singleton et al., 2007.

claim: Hexameric helicases assort into two main groups: bacterial helicases (SF4,5) with ATP sites derived from the RecA fold and eukaryotic/archaeal helicases (SF3,6) with ATP sites derived from the AAA+ fold.
source: There are four superfamilies of hexameric helicases, SF3-6, that assort into two main groups, the bacterial helicases (SF4,5) that have ATP sites derived from the RecA fold and the eukaryotic/archaeal helicases (SF3,6) that have ATP sites derived from the AAA+ fold (Singleton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singleton et al., 2007.

claim: Subunits of hexameric helicases are composed of at least two major domains, giving them the appearance of two stacked rings, an N-tier ring and C-tier ring.
source: In all cases, the subunits of hexameric helicases are composed of at least two major domains, giving them the appearance of two stacked rings, an N-tier ring and C-tier ring; the motors are contained in the C-tier ring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about helicase structure.

claim: The motors of hexameric helicases are contained in the C-tier ring.
source: In all cases, the subunits of hexameric helicases are composed of at least two major domains, giving them the appearance of two stacked rings, an N-tier ring and C-tier ring; the motors are contained in the C-tier ring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about helicase structure.

claim: RecA based bacterial helicases track 5'−3' on DNA with the C-tier motors leading the N-tier.
source: The RecA based bacterial helicases track 5'−3' on DNA with the C-tier motors leading the N-tier, as determined by crystal structures of bacterial Rho (SF5) and DnaB (SF4) complexed with ssDNA, while structures of eukaryotic bovine papilloma virus E1 (SF3) and S. cerevisiae CMG (SF6) with DNA show that these helicases track 3'−5' with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Georgescu et al., 2017; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012; Thomsen and Berger, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures of Rho and DnaB.

claim: Eukaryotic helicases E1 and CMG track 3'−5' with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier.
source: The RecA based bacterial helicases track 5'−3' on DNA with the C-tier motors leading the N-tier, as determined by crystal structures of bacterial Rho (SF5) and DnaB (SF4) complexed with ssDNA, while structures of eukaryotic bovine papilloma virus E1 (SF3) and S. cerevisiae CMG (SF6) with DNA show that these helicases track 3'−5' with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Georgescu et al., 2017; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012; Thomsen and Berger, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structures of E1 and CMG.

claim: Hexameric helicases act by encircling only one strand of DNA upon which they track and exclude the non-tracking strand to the outside of the ring.
source: Hexameric helicases are thought to act by encircling only one strand of DNA upon which they track and exclude the non-tracking strand to the outside of the ring, thereby acting as a wedge to split DNA in a process often referred to as steric exclusion and illustrated in Figure 1A (Bell and Labib, 2016; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Lyubimov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: For a steric exclusion helicase, a block placed on the non-tracking strand does not inhibit helicase unwinding.
source: For a steric exclusion helicase, a block placed on the non-tracking strand (i.e. the strand that is excluded from the central channel) does not inhibit helicase unwinding, while a block placed on the tracking strand stops the helicase because the bulky block cannot fit through the central channel.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the steric exclusion mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: For a steric exclusion helicase, a block placed on the tracking strand stops the helicase because the bulky block cannot fit through the central channel.
source: For a steric exclusion helicase, a block placed on the non-tracking strand (i.e. the strand that is excluded from the central channel) does not inhibit helicase unwinding, while a block placed on the tracking strand stops the helicase because the bulky block cannot fit through the central channel.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the steric exclusion mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: The eukaryotic helicase is the Mcm2-7 heterohexamer which requires five additional accessory proteins - Cdc45 and the four subunit GINS complex – for full activity.
source: The eukaryotic helicase is the Mcm2-7 heterohexamer which requires five additional accessory proteins - Cdc45 and the four subunit GINS complex – for full activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the eukaryotic replicative helicase supported by citations.

claim: The 11-subunit assembly of Mcm2-7, Cdc45, and GINS is referred to as CMG.
source: This 11-subunit assembly is referred to as CMG (Cdc45, Mcm2-7, GINS) (Ilves et al., 2010; Moyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ilves et al., 2010 and Moyer et al., 2006.

claim: The cryoEM 3D structure of S. cerevisiae CMG helicase at a DNA replication fork shows that zinc fingers of the N-tier encircle and bind the dsDNA.
source: The recent cryoEM 3D structure of S. cerevisiae CMG helicase at a DNA replication fork shows a unique DNA binding feature (Figure 1B) (Georgescu et al., 2017). Instead of encircling only ssDNA, the zinc fingers of the N-tier encircle and bind the dsDNA and the DNA unwinding point is buried inside the central channel; the unwound leading strand then proceeds through the central channel into the C-tier motor domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the CMG-DNA structure, the DNA unwinding point is buried inside the central channel.
source: Instead of encircling only ssDNA, the zinc fingers of the N-tier encircle and bind the dsDNA and the DNA unwinding point is buried inside the central channel; the unwound leading strand then proceeds through the central channel into the C-tier motor domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2017 and structural data.

claim: The unwound leading strand proceeds through the central channel into the C-tier motor domain of CMG.
source: Instead of encircling only ssDNA, the zinc fingers of the N-tier encircle and bind the dsDNA and the DNA unwinding point is buried inside the central channel; the unwound leading strand then proceeds through the central channel into the C-tier motor domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2017 and structural data.

claim: The lagging strand is not visualized in the CMG-DNA structure, indicating mobility.
source: The lagging strand is not visualized in the structure, indicating mobility, and is proposed to enter the initial part of the central channel defined by the N-terminal zinc fingers and then exit the surface of CMG, through a gap between two zinc fingers.
evidence: This is an inference from structural data where the lagging strand is not visible.

claim: The lagging strand is proposed to enter the initial part of the central channel defined by the N-terminal zinc fingers and then exit the surface of CMG through a gap between two zinc fingers.
source: The lagging strand is not visualized in the structure, indicating mobility, and is proposed to enter the initial part of the central channel defined by the N-terminal zinc fingers and then exit the surface of CMG, through a gap between two zinc fingers.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on structural data.

claim: The dsDNA is held at a 28° angle to the central channel of CMG, surrounded by the zinc fingers at the 'top' of CMG.
source: The dsDNA is held at a 28° angle to the central channel, surrounded by the zinc fingers at the 'top' of CMG.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from Georgescu et al., 2017.

claim: The dsDNA appears to be tightly held by CMG because if the CMG-dsDNA contact was flexible the DNA would have been averaged out during 3D reconstruction.
source: The dsDNA appears to be tightly held because if the CMG-dsDNA contact was flexible the DNA would have been averaged out during 3D reconstruction.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural biology principles.

claim: Biochemical experiments using strand specific dual streptavidin blocks show CMG is halted by a block placed on either the non-tracking (lagging) or the tracking (leading) strand.
source: The structural evidence that S. cerevisiae CMG encircles dsDNA during unwinding is supported by recent biochemical experiments using strand specific dual streptavidin blocks that show CMG is halted by a block placed on either the non-tracking (lagging) or the tracking (leading) strand (Figure 1C) (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Langston and O'Donnell, 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Given sufficient time, S. cerevisiae CMG can proceed through the lagging strand block without displacing the streptavidin.
source: Interestingly, given a sufficiently long time S. cerevisiae CMG can proceed through the lagging strand block without displacing the streptavidin, suggesting that CMG slowly isomerizes to a classic steric exclusion mode that only encircles the tracking (leading) strand or isomerizes by ring opening to bypass the block (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Langston and O'Donnell, 2017.

claim: CMG slowly isomerizes to a classic steric exclusion mode that only encircles the tracking (leading) strand or isomerizes by ring opening to bypass the block.
source: Interestingly, given a sufficiently long time S. cerevisiae CMG can proceed through the lagging strand block without displacing the streptavidin, suggesting that CMG slowly isomerizes to a classic steric exclusion mode that only encircles the tracking (leading) strand or isomerizes by ring opening to bypass the block (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data from Langston and O'Donnell, 2017.

claim: Studies in Xenopus extracts demonstrate that replisome progression is not hindered by a dual streptavidin block on the lagging strand.
source: Earlier studies in Xenopus extracts demonstrate that replisome progression is not hindered by a dual streptavidin block on the lagging strand and conclude that CMG functions in a steric exclusion mode by only encircling the leading strand (Fu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2011.

claim: Xenopus extracts contain a factor that facilitates isomerization of CMG on DNA such that it can bypass blocks on the non-tracking strand.
source: Considering that the zinc fingers of isolated S. cerevisiae CMG encircle dsDNA, we proposed that Xenopus extracts contain a factor that facilitates isomerization of CMG on DNA such that it can bypass blocks on the non-tracking strand (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is a proposal based on inference from comparing isolated CMG behavior to Xenopus extract behavior.

claim: Mcm10 is the factor that enables CMG to rapidly bypass a block on the lagging strand.
source: The present study identifies Mcm10 as the factor that enables CMG to rapidly bypass a block on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript, particularly Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mcm10 is an essential gene product that, when mutated, causes abortive entry into S-phase.
source: Mcm10 is unique to eukaryotes and is an essential gene product that, when mutated, causes abortive entry into S-phase (Du et al., 2012; Merchant et al., 1997; Solomon et al., 1992; Thu and Bielinsky, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mcm10 has two internal DNA binding sites.
source: Mcm10 has two internal DNA binding sites (Du et al., 2012; Robertson et al., 2008; Warren et al., 2008) and is known to bind Mcm2-7 and Cdc45 (Christensen and Tye, 2003; Di Perna et al., 2013; Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Perez-Arnaiz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du et al., 2012; Robertson et al., 2008; Warren et al., 2008.

claim: Mcm10 is known to bind Mcm2-7 and Cdc45.
source: Mcm10 has two internal DNA binding sites (Du et al., 2012; Robertson et al., 2008; Warren et al., 2008) and is known to bind Mcm2-7 and Cdc45 (Christensen and Tye, 2003; Di Perna et al., 2013; Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Perez-Arnaiz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Christensen and Tye, 2003; Di Perna et al., 2013; Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Perez-Arnaiz et al., 2016.

claim: Mcm10 is generally thought to act as an initiation factor.
source: Mcm10 is generally thought to act as an initiation factor (Thu and Bielinsky, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thu and Bielinsky, 2013.

claim: Mcm10 is not required for transformation of the Mcm2-7 double hexamer into two head-to-head CMGs during S phase.
source: Additional initiation factors transform the Mcm2-7 double hexamer into two head-to-head CMGs during S phase (Bell and Labib, 2016) but Mcm10 is not required for this action (Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015.

claim: Mcm10 is only required at the last step of initiation.
source: Mcm10 is only required at the last step of initiation and is proposed to either activate CMG helicase or help separate the two CMGs for bidirectional replication forks (Kanke et al., 2012; Lõoke et al., 2017; Quan et al., 2015; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mcm10 is proposed to either activate CMG helicase or help separate the two CMGs for bidirectional replication forks.
source: Mcm10 is only required at the last step of initiation and is proposed to either activate CMG helicase or help separate the two CMGs for bidirectional replication forks (Kanke et al., 2012; Lõoke et al., 2017; Quan et al., 2015; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal based on citations to multiple studies.

claim: Studies indicate that Mcm10 may also function at replication forks.
source: Additional studies indicate that Mcm10 may also function at replication forks (Chadha et al., 2016; Gambus et al., 2006; Lõoke et al., 2017; Ricke and Bielinsky, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chadha et al., 2016; Gambus et al., 2006; Lõoke et al., 2017; Ricke and Bielinsky, 2004.

claim: Mcm10 forms an isolable stoichiometric complex with CMG.
source: The current study demonstrates that Mcm10 forms an isolable stoichiometric complex with CMG that greatly stimulates CMG helicase activity (up to 30-fold) and enhances processivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: Mcm10 greatly stimulates CMG helicase activity up to 30-fold.
source: The current study demonstrates that Mcm10 forms an isolable stoichiometric complex with CMG that greatly stimulates CMG helicase activity (up to 30-fold) and enhances processivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Mcm10 enhances processivity of CMG helicase.
source: The current study demonstrates that Mcm10 forms an isolable stoichiometric complex with CMG that greatly stimulates CMG helicase activity (up to 30-fold) and enhances processivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Mcm10 uniquely promotes CMG bypass of a lagging strand block without displacing it.
source: Strikingly, Mcm10 uniquely promotes CMG bypass of a lagging strand block without displacing it, suggesting that Mcm10 isomerizes the CMG-DNA complex either to a steric exclusion mode or by facilitating ring opening.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mcm10 isomerizes the CMG-DNA complex either to a steric exclusion mode or by facilitating ring opening.
source: Strikingly, Mcm10 uniquely promotes CMG bypass of a lagging strand block without displacing it, suggesting that Mcm10 isomerizes the CMG-DNA complex either to a steric exclusion mode or by facilitating ring opening.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the bypass data.

claim: Leading strand blocks inhibit CMG unwinding.
source: In contrast, leading strand blocks inhibit CMG unwinding but Mcm10 helps CMG displace the blocks and continue unwinding, consistent with the idea that Mcm10 makes CMG a more powerful, processive helicase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mcm10 helps CMG displace leading strand blocks and continue unwinding.
source: In contrast, leading strand blocks inhibit CMG unwinding but Mcm10 helps CMG displace the blocks and continue unwinding, consistent with the idea that Mcm10 makes CMG a more powerful, processive helicase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Mcm10 makes CMG a more powerful, processive helicase.
source: In contrast, leading strand blocks inhibit CMG unwinding but Mcm10 helps CMG displace the blocks and continue unwinding, consistent with the idea that Mcm10 makes CMG a more powerful, processive helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of Mcm10 to help CMG displace leading strand blocks.

claim: Mcm10 has little effect on CMG-dependent DNA synthesis by the replisome in vitro, particularly in the presence of the Mrc1-Tof1-Csm3 complex.
source: Despite the strong stimulation of helicase activity, Mcm10 has little effect on CMG-dependent DNA synthesis by the replisome in vitro, particularly in the presence of the Mrc1-Tof1-Csm3 complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: The replisome becomes stalled by lagging strand blocks in the absence of Mcm10.
source: However, the replisome becomes stalled by lagging strand blocks in the absence of Mcm10, indicating that CMG uses an internal unwinding mechanism even in the context of rapidly moving replisomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: CMG uses an internal unwinding mechanism even in the context of rapidly moving replisomes.
source: However, the replisome becomes stalled by lagging strand blocks in the absence of Mcm10, indicating that CMG uses an internal unwinding mechanism even in the context of rapidly moving replisomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lagging strand blocks stall the replisome.

claim: Stalled replisomes are released by addition of Mcm10.
source: Stalled replisomes are released by addition of Mcm10, further supporting the idea that Mcm10 functions at the level of the helicase to enhance processivity, provide additional power and to enable blocked replisomes to bypass obstacles on the DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Mcm10 functions at the level of the helicase to enhance processivity, provide additional power and to enable blocked replisomes to bypass obstacles on the DNA.
source: Stalled replisomes are released by addition of Mcm10, further supporting the idea that Mcm10 functions at the level of the helicase to enhance processivity, provide additional power and to enable blocked replisomes to bypass obstacles on the DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Mcm10 releases stalled replisomes.

claim: Mcm10 deficiency leads to genome instability and increased dependence on post-replication and recombinational repair pathways to maintain viability.
source: The function of Mcm10 in facilitating replisome bypass of lagging strand blocks is consistent with genetic studies showing that Mcm10 deficiency leads to genome instability and increased dependence on post-replication and recombinational repair pathways to maintain viability (Araki et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Araki et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2010.

claim: The internal DNA binding region of Xenopus Mcm10 has two DNA binding elements, an OB fold and a zinc finger, that allow it to bind ssDNA and/or dsDNA.
source: Previous reports have solved the structure of the internal DNA binding region of Xenopus Mcm10 and documented that the internal region has two DNA binding elements, an OB fold and a zinc finger, that allow it to bind ssDNA and/or dsDNA (Du et al., 2012; Robertson et al., 2008; Warren et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du et al., 2012; Robertson et al., 2008; Warren et al., 2008.

claim: The C-terminal region of Mcm10 forms the main interaction site to Mcms.
source: Following the internal DNA binding region is a C-terminal region that forms the main interaction site to Mcms (Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Lõoke et al., 2017; Quan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Douglas and Diffley, 2016; Lõoke et al., 2017; Quan et al., 2015.

claim: Mcm10 appears to bind to the N-tier region of the CMG complex that faces the forked junction.
source: Furthermore, Mcm10 appears to bind to the N-tier region of the CMG complex that faces the forked junction (Figure 1B), as recent studies show that interaction of Mcm10 with Mcm2-7 is mediated primarily through an interaction with a conserved domain in the N-terminal region of the Mcm2 subunit (Lõoke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lõoke et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Interaction of Mcm10 with Mcm2-7 is mediated primarily through an interaction with a conserved domain in the N-terminal region of the Mcm2 subunit.
source: Furthermore, Mcm10 appears to bind to the N-tier region of the CMG complex that faces the forked junction (Figure 1B), as recent studies show that interaction of Mcm10 with Mcm2-7 is mediated primarily through an interaction with a conserved domain in the N-terminal region of the Mcm2 subunit (Lõoke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lõoke et al., 2017.

claim: Upon encountering a lagging strand block, Mcm10 binds at the N-tier of CMG and also binds DNA at the fork.
source: Consistent with these known properties of Mcm10, we propose in Figure 7 that, upon encountering a lagging strand block, Mcm10 binds at the N-tier of CMG and also binds DNA at the fork.
evidence: This is a proposal based on known properties of Mcm10 and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Mcm10 binding places Mcm10 between CMG and the forked junction such that duplex DNA no longer enters the zinc fingers that line the top of the central channel of CMG.
source: This places Mcm10 between CMG and the forked junction such that duplex DNA no longer enters the zinc fingers that line the top of the central channel of CMG.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the proposed configuration, Mcm10 isomerizes CMG to a steric exclusion mode where it is capable of bypassing blocks on the non-tracking strand.
source: In this configuration, Mcm10 isomerizes CMG to a steric exclusion mode where it is capable of bypassing blocks on the non-tracking strand as observed with other hexameric helicases and with the complete replisome in the Xenopus extract system (Fu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the bypass data and comparison to other helicases.

claim: Alternative isomerization reactions that would facilitate lagging strand block bypass include Mcm10 cracking open the N-tier of the Mcm2-7 ring of CMG, bypassing the block, and reclosing the N-tier.
source: Two alternative isomerization reactions that would also facilitate lagging strand block bypass without displacement include one in which Mcm10 cracks open the N-tier of the Mcm2-7 ring of CMG, bypasses the block, and recloses the N-tier.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for an alternative mechanism.

claim: Mcm10 might enable opening of both the N- and C-tiers, either simultaneously or in succession, to bypass the blocks.
source: Similarly, Mcm10 might enable opening of both the N- and C-tiers, either simultaneously or in succession, to bypass the blocks.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for an alternative mechanism.

claim: CMG evolved a requirement for another protein to bypass a lagging strand block for regulation of fork initiation and progression.
source: One possible reason that CMG evolved a requirement for another protein to bypass a lagging strand block is for regulation of fork initiation and progression.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about evolutionary reasons.

claim: The head-to-head double hexamer of Mcm2-7 at an origin matures to form two CMGs on dsDNA without unwinding DNA.
source: It is documented from several laboratories that the head-to-head (N-to-N) double hexamer of Mcm2-7 at an origin matures to form two CMGs on dsDNA without unwinding DNA (Heller et al., 2011; Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mcm10 is required at the last step of origin initiation to 'activate' CMG to unwind DNA as detected by RPA binding to the ssDNA products.
source: Mcm10 is required at the last step of origin initiation to 'activate' CMG to unwind DNA as detected by RPA binding to the ssDNA products.
evidence: This is supported by citations mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: CMG tracks with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier.
source: Specifically, CMG is known to track with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier, and therefore head-to-head CMGs at an origin are directed inward toward one another.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CMG structure and function.

claim: Head-to-head CMGs at an origin are directed inward toward one another, so each CMG blocks the other CMG at an origin.
source: Specifically, CMG is known to track with the N-tier ahead of the C-tier, and therefore head-to-head CMGs at an origin are directed inward toward one another. Hence, each CMG blocks the other CMG at an origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the known structure and orientation of CMG.

claim: If Mcm10 activates the CMGs to locally unwind DNA, the two CMGs could isomerize to encircle opposite single-strands and pass one another to form bidirectional forks.
source: However, if Mcm10 activates the CMGs to locally unwind DNA, as observed by head-to-head SV40 T-antigen hexamers that produce ssDNA 'rabbit ears' at the viral origin (Wessel et al., 1992), the two CMGs could isomerize to encircle opposite single-strands and pass one another to form bidirectional forks (see Figure 8B in [Georgescu et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on analogy to SV40 T-antigen and supported by citation.

claim: Mcm10 may not be required at all times during replication considering that it does not appear to increase the elongation rate of the replisome.
source: Considering that Mcm10 does not appear to increase the elongation rate of the replisome (Figure 4C), it may not be required at all times.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 4C.

claim: Mcm10 might only be needed to help the replisome bypass blocks on the lagging strand which could be performed by a dynamic Mcm10 that interacts only transiently with a stalled replisome.
source: For example, Mcm10 might only be needed to help the replisome bypass blocks on the lagging strand which conceivably could be performed by a dynamic Mcm10 that interacts only transiently with a stalled replisome.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about Mcm10 dynamics.

claim: Mcm10 mediated isomerization of CMG-DNA may remain stable, in which case Mcm10 may not be needed for some time after its first use.
source: Alternatively, Mcm10 mediated isomerization of CMG-DNA may remain stable, in which case Mcm10 may not be needed for some time after its first use, and in fact an Mcm10 effect on CMG that only requires transient Mcm10 binding has been demonstrated in an earlier study (Lõoke et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by citation to Lõoke et al., 2017.

claim: Mcm10 binds remarkably tightly to CMG, eluting as a CMG-Mcm10 complex from beads after high salt washes.
source: Mcm10 binds remarkably tightly to CMG, eluting as a CMG-Mcm10 complex from beads after high salt washes (Figure 2D), and the CMG-Mcm10 complex also remains associated and elutes from a MonoQ ion-exchange resin at high ionic strength (400–450 mM NaCl) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The CMG-Mcm10 complex remains associated and elutes from a MonoQ ion-exchange resin at high ionic strength (400–450 mM NaCl).
source: Mcm10 binds remarkably tightly to CMG, eluting as a CMG-Mcm10 complex from beads after high salt washes (Figure 2D), and the CMG-Mcm10 complex also remains associated and elutes from a MonoQ ion-exchange resin at high ionic strength (400–450 mM NaCl) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Some studies suggest Mcm10 is a component of moving replisomes.
source: Additionally, some studies suggest Mcm10 is a component of moving replisomes (Chadha et al., 2016; Gambus et al., 2006; Lõoke et al., 2017; Ricke and Bielinsky, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chadha et al., 2016; Gambus et al., 2006; Lõoke et al., 2017; Ricke and Bielinsky, 2004.

claim: Other cellular studies indicate that Mcm10 is not in constant association with the replisome.
source: However, other cellular studies indicate that Mcm10 is not in constant association with the replisome (Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanke et al., 2012; van Deursen et al., 2012; Watase et al., 2012.

claim: Mcm10 stimulation of CMG is over 30-fold enhancement at 2 minutes in the presence of only one molecule of Mcm10 per CMG.
source: Stimulation by Mcm10 is remarkable, with over 30-fold enhancement of CMG unwinding at 2' in the presence of only one molecule of Mcm10 per CMG (compare lane 5 to lane 2 in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: Reactions containing Mcm10 are complete by the 5 min time point, while the CMG reaction without Mcm10 continues slow unwinding during the 10 min time course.
source: Reactions containing Mcm10 are complete by the 5 min time point, while the CMG reaction without Mcm10 continues slow unwinding during the 10 min time course (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Maximal stimulation of CMG is observed with two subunits of Mcm10 for each CMG complex.
source: The results at different Mcm10 concentrations indicate that maximal stimulation of CMG is observed with two subunits of Mcm10 for each CMG complex and further addition of Mcm10 beyond this amount has little effect. (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: Mcm10 alone, lacking CMG, shows no unwinding activity.
source: Control reactions with Mcm10 alone, lacking CMG, show no unwinding activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stimulation of CMG is specific to Mcm10 and RPA and SSB do not substitute for Mcm10.
source: The results show that the stimulation of CMG is specific to Mcm10 and that RPA and SSB do not substitute for Mcm10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Densitometric analysis of CMG-Mcm10 complex indicates a molar ratio of 1.8 Mcm10 per Mcm2-7 complex.
source: A densitometric scan of the bands in the gel of the CMG-Mcm10 complex indicates a molar ratio of 1.8 Mcm10 per Mcm2-7 complex; the Cdc45 is typically in excess due to the Flag tag (i.e. any dissociated Cdc45 will bind the beads).
evidence: This is demonstrated by densitometric analysis of the gel in Figure 2D.

claim: Densitometric scans from several preparations of CMG-Mcm10 give a stoichiometry of ~1–2 Mcm10 subunits for each CMG complex.
source: Densitometric scans from several preparations of CMG-Mcm10 made using both methods give a stoichiometry of ~1–2 Mcm10 subunits for each CMG complex, consistent with the Mcm10 titration results of Figure 2A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by densitometric analysis of multiple preparations.

claim: CMG unwound only 3% of the longer 160 bp duplex fork in 10 minutes in the absence of Mcm10.
source: CMG unwound only 3% of the longer 160 bp duplex fork in 10' (Figure 3B lanes 1–10 and graph in Figure 3D) compared to 24% for the shorter 50 bp duplex fork at 10' (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: CMG unwound 24% of the shorter 50 bp duplex fork at 10 minutes in the absence of Mcm10.
source: CMG unwound only 3% of the longer 160 bp duplex fork in 10' (Figure 3B lanes 1–10 and graph in Figure 3D) compared to 24% for the shorter 50 bp duplex fork at 10' (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3C.

claim: After 30 minutes only 8% of the 160 bp duplex was unwound by CMG indicating that the difference in activity between the two substrates is attributable to low processivity of CMG.
source: Even after 30' only 8% of the 160 bp duplex was unwound by CMG indicating that the difference in activity between the two substrates is attributable to low processivity of CMG rather than simply the additional time it takes to unwind the longer substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data and interpreted as evidence of low processivity.

claim: In the presence of Mcm10 the unwinding curves of the 50 bp and 160 bp substrates were very similar, in contrast to experiments in the absence of Mcm10.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of Mcm10 the unwinding curves of the two substrates were very similar, in contrast to experiments in the absence of Mcm10 (Figure 3B and C, lanes 11–19 and graph in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B, 3C, and 3D.

claim: Mcm10 enhances the processivity of CMG and possibly also stimulates the rate of CMG unwinding.
source: This result suggests that Mcm10 enhances the processivity of CMG and possibly also stimulates the rate of CMG unwinding.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar unwinding curves for different length substrates in the presence of Mcm10.

claim: Appearance of unwound 160 bp duplex products was delayed by ~46 s compared to the 50 bp duplex, indicating an average rate of unwinding of 2.4 bp/s over the additional 110 bp.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, appearance of unwound 160 bp duplex products was delayed by ~46 s compared to the 50 bp duplex, indicating an average rate of unwinding of 2.4 bp/s over the additional 110 bp.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of Mcm10 the 2.8 kb full length product can be observed at the 6 minute time point, yielding a maximum fork rate of 7.8 nucleotides/s (467 ntds/min).
source: In the presence of Mcm10 the 2.8 kb full length product can be observed at the 6' time point (Figure 4B, lanes 8 and 13), yielding a maximum fork rate of 7.8 nucleotides (ntds)/s; 467 ntds/min), while 8' is required to observe the full-length product in the absence of Mcm10 (Figure 4B, lane 4; 5.8 ntds/s; 350 ntds/min).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: 8 minutes is required to observe the full-length product in the absence of Mcm10, corresponding to a fork rate of 5.8 ntds/s (350 ntds/min).
source: In the presence of Mcm10 the 2.8 kb full length product can be observed at the 6' time point (Figure 4B, lanes 8 and 13), yielding a maximum fork rate of 7.8 nucleotides (ntds)/s; 467 ntds/min), while 8' is required to observe the full-length product in the absence of Mcm10 (Figure 4B, lane 4; 5.8 ntds/s; 350 ntds/min).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Replication forks move about 2-fold slower in cells that lack Mrc1.
source: Cell biological and genetic studies have shown that replication forks move about 2-fold slower in cells that lack Mrc1 (Hodgson et al., 2007; Petermann et al., 2008; Szyjka et al., 2005; Tourrière et al., 2005) and these observations have been recapitulated in vitro in a origin plasmid replication system (Yeeles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hodgson et al., 2007; Petermann et al., 2008; Szyjka et al., 2005; Tourrière et al., 2005.

claim: Mrc1 stimulation of fork speed was most efficient in the presence of a Tof1-Csm3 heterodimeric complex.
source: The in vitro results demonstrated that Mrc1 stimulation of fork speed was most efficient in the presence of a Tof1-Csm3 heterodimeric complex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeeles et al., 2017.

claim: In the presence of the MTC complex, full length 2.8 kb product can be observed after 3 min, indicating a rate of 20 ntds/s (933 ntds/min).
source: The autoradiogram shows that in the presence of the MTC complex, full length 2.8 kb product can be observed after 3 min (Figure 4C, lane 6), indicating a rate of 20 ntds/s (933 ntds/min), close to the 1.5–1.9 kb/min rate of replisomes in vivo (Conti et al., 2007; Hodgson et al., 2007; Sekedat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: The rate of 20 ntds/s (933 ntds/min) with MTC complex is close to the 1.5–1.9 kb/min rate of replisomes in vivo.
source: The autoradiogram shows that in the presence of the MTC complex, full length 2.8 kb product can be observed after 3 min (Figure 4C, lane 6), indicating a rate of 20 ntds/s (933 ntds/min), close to the 1.5–1.9 kb/min rate of replisomes in vivo (Conti et al., 2007; Hodgson et al., 2007; Sekedat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conti et al., 2007; Hodgson et al., 2007; Sekedat et al., 2010.

claim: The MTC complex clears up the many immature products formed in the absence of MTC, suggesting that replication forks that stop or pause are brought to full length by the MTC complex.
source: Furthermore, the MTC complex clears up the many immature products formed in the absence of MTC, suggesting that replication forks that stop or pause are brought to full length by the MTC complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: Addition of Mcm10 to leading strand replisome reactions containing the MTC complex does not result in a faster replication fork rate and may have even slightly slowed the replisome.
source: Addition of Mcm10 to leading strand replisome reactions containing the MTC complex does not result in a faster replication fork rate under the conditions used and may have even slightly slowed the replisome (Figure 4C, lanes 11–15).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: The improved rate effect of Mcm10 on the core leading strand replisome is eclipsed by the rate enhancement provided by the MTC complex.
source: Thus, the improved rate effect of Mcm10 on the core leading strand replisome observed in Figure 4B is eclipsed by the rate enhancement provided by the MTC complex.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Mcm10 is required for efficient initiation of DNA unwinding at an origin, a situation in which the two CMG complexes block one another's progression.
source: Indeed, Mcm10 is required for efficient initiation of DNA unwinding at an origin, a situation in which the two CMG complexes block one another's progression because they must pass each other in order to establish two bidirectional forks (see Discussion) (Georgescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2017.

claim: CMG unwinding is inhibited by biotin-streptavidin on either strand and is nearly inactive when two biotin-streptavidin blocks are present on either strand of the duplex.
source: We recently showed that CMG unwinding is inhibited by biotin-streptavidin on either strand and is nearly inactive when two biotin-streptavidin blocks are present on either strand of the duplex (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Langston and O'Donnell, 2017.

claim: CMG being blocked by an obstruction on the non-tracking strand is unique to CMG, as all other hexameric helicases examined are not blocked by an obstruction on the non-tracking strand.
source: This is unique to CMG, as thus far all other hexameric helicases examined are not blocked by an obstruction on the non-tracking strand and are only blocked by an obstruction on the translocating strand (Hacker and Johnson, 1997; Kaplan, 2000; Kaplan et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2014; Nakano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hacker and Johnson, 1997; Kaplan, 2000; Kaplan et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2014; Nakano et al., 2013.

claim: CMG helicase is essentially shut down by streptavidin blocks on the lagging strand in the absence of Mcm10.
source: Control reactions lacking Mcm10 show that CMG helicase is essentially shut down by the streptavidin blocks (Figure 5B, compare lanes 2–4 without streptavidin to lanes 5–7 with streptavidin) as previously observed (Langston and O'Donnell, 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B and supported by citation.

claim: When Mcm10 is added, the rate and amount of unwinding are the same in the presence and absence of streptavidin on the lagging strand.
source: But surprisingly, when Mcm10 is added, the rate and amount of unwinding are the same in the presence and absence of streptavidin (Figure 5B, compare lanes 8–10 and 11–13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B.

claim: Mcm10 enables CMG to rapidly bypass or displace a dual streptavidin block on the lagging strand.
source: Hence, Mcm10 enables CMG to rapidly bypass or displace a dual streptavidin block on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5B.

claim: MTC was unable to promote CMG bypass of the lagging strand block.
source: In contrast to Mcm10, MTC was unable to promote CMG bypass of the block (compare lanes 11–13 in Figure 5C to lanes 11–13 in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: MTC did not stimulate CMG unwinding even in the absence of the block.
source: We also note that MTC did not stimulate CMG unwinding even in the absence of the block (Figure 5C compare lanes 8–10 with MTC to lanes 2–4 without MTC), suggesting that MTC does not function at the level of CMG unwinding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: MTC does not function at the level of CMG unwinding.
source: We also note that MTC did not stimulate CMG unwinding even in the absence of the block (Figure 5C compare lanes 8–10 with MTC to lanes 2–4 without MTC), suggesting that MTC does not function at the level of CMG unwinding.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: Mcm10 and MTC affect fork progression in very different ways.
source: Together with the results of Figures 2–4, these data suggest that Mcm10 and MTC affect fork progression in very different ways.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the effects of Mcm10 and MTC across multiple experiments.

claim: CMG unwinding was delayed and strongly repressed by a dual streptavidin block on the leading strand even with Mcm10 present.
source: In contrast to Mcm10 mediated bypass of lagging strand blocks, CMG unwinding was delayed and strongly repressed by a dual streptavidin block on the leading strand even with Mcm10 present (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pol ε-PCNA extended the primer to the stalled CMG (~66 bp) but had limited ability to bypass the block to form the 141 bp full-length product.
source: The results in Figure 5E lanes 1–3 show that Pol ε-PCNA extended the 32P-primer to the stalled CMG (~66 bp) but had limited ability to bypass the block to form the 141 bp full-length product.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: The ~91 bp bands result from forks lacking CMG, so Pol ε-PCNA extends to the fork but cannot proceed further because Pol ε lacks strand displacement capability.
source: The ~91 bp bands result from forks lacking CMG, so Pol ε-PCNA extends to the fork but cannot proceed further because Pol ε lacks strand displacement capability and relies on CMG to unwind the DNA for leading strand synthesis (Ganai et al., 2016; Georgescu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: MTC has little or no effect on block bypass by the replisome.
source: MTC has little or no effect on block bypass by the replisome (Figure 5E lanes 7–9), and is comparable to Pol ε-PCNA-CMG in lanes 1–3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Addition of Mcm10 allows the replisome to efficiently and rapidly proceed past lagging strand blocks as evidenced by the appearance of full length 141 bp product.
source: By contrast, addition of Mcm10 allows the replisome to efficiently and rapidly proceed past these blocks as evidenced by the appearance of full length 141 bp product in lanes 4–6.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Mcm10 is needed for replisome bypass of a block.
source: These results confirm that Mcm10 is needed for replisome bypass of a block and they also indicate that neither MTC nor Pol ε-PCNA is able to drive the forward movement of a stalled CMG in the absence of Mcm10.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Neither MTC nor Pol ε-PCNA is able to drive the forward movement of a stalled CMG in the absence of Mcm10.
source: These results confirm that Mcm10 is needed for replisome bypass of a block and they also indicate that neither MTC nor Pol ε-PCNA is able to drive the forward movement of a stalled CMG in the absence of Mcm10.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Nearly all of the unwound product DNA retains the streptavidin when CMG-Mcm10 bypasses lagging strand blocks.
source: Upon performing the experiment using dual biotinylated-streptavidin blocks on the lagging strand template, the results show that nearly all of the unwound product DNA retains the streptavidin (i.e. it is gel shifted) in the presence of the excess biotin trap.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6A.

claim: CMG-Mcm10 bypasses lagging strand streptavidin blocks without displacing them from DNA.
source: Hence, CMG-Mcm10 bypasses lagging strand streptavidin blocks without displacing them from DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 6A showing streptavidin remains bound.

claim: Streptavidin is displaced from the unwound product when CMG-Mcm10 encounters leading strand blocks.
source: The results demonstrate that streptavidin is displaced from the unwound product (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Mcm10 appears to provide CMG with more translocation force than CMG alone.
source: Hence, Mcm10 appears to provide CMG with more translocation force than CMG alone, consistent with the increase in processivity of CMG in the presence of Mcm10 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of CMG-Mcm10 to displace leading strand blocks.
